_**User**_

Clean up first. Remove left vertices with fewer than θ neighbors total, since they can never qualify. Remove right vertices that then have no left neighbors. Repeat until nothing changes.
Pick a starting right vertex. Try the ones touching the most left vertices first. Your group starts as just that vertex, and your candidate pool is everything similar to it.
Repeatedly add one candidate to the group. After each addition, the candidate pool shrinks to only vertices similar to everything in the group, which guarantees the group stays all-pairs similar. To choose which candidate to add, favor the one that helps the most left vertices, weighting more heavily those that are closest to reaching θ neighbors in the group.
Prune hopeless branches. A left vertex is still “alive” if its neighbors already in the group plus its neighbors still in the candidate pool could reach θ. The number of alive left vertices is an upper bound on what this branch can achieve, so if it’s no better than your best answer so far, stop and move to the next starting vertex.
Keep the best result across all starting vertices. The core is all left vertices with at least θ neighbors in the final group.

Can you implement this as a heuristic to find the largest epsilon-cohesive core and then test it using the overlap coefficient.

The algorithm has two phases. First, iteratively prune left vertices with fewer than θ neighbors and any right vertices that lose all left neighbors. Second, search by starting from right vertices that touch the most left vertices, then repeatedly add similar candidates to expand each group.

After each addition, the candidate pool shrinks to vertices similar to every member of the group. The next candidate is chosen to maximize the number of left vertices that can reach θ neighbors. A left vertex stays alive if its remaining neighbors could still reach θ once added. If a branch cannot exceed the best result found so far, it prunes and the search moves to the next starting vertex.

The heuristic is in `src/heuristic.jl`, and the overlap-coefficient tests all pass.

`cohesive_core(g, theta, epsilon, metric)` peels the graph, then grows one all-pairs-similar right-hand group from each surviving right vertex. Seeds are tried highest left-degree first. The candidate added next is the one that helps the most left vertices still short of θ, and a vertex that already has `hits` neighbors in the group counts as `hits + 1`, so a vertex one step from θ outweighs one that has none. After each addition the pool shrinks to vertices similar to every member of the group. A branch stops when the number of left vertices that could still reach θ is no larger than the best core so far. The core is every left vertex with at least θ neighbors in the final group.

Similar means distance ≤ `epsilon`, the same test `map_graph` uses. Peeling runs on a copy, so `overlap_metric(g)` still reads the original neighborhoods. Buyers below θ can never join a core, but they still count toward the overlap coefficient.

The tests are `julia --project=. test/heuristic.jl`. On the overlap graphs, the core matched an exhaustive enumeration of every right-hand subset:

- A popular item is tried first. Its private neighbors have overlap distance 0 with it and 1 with each other, so they never form one group. A later biclique of 3 users is the core.
- Two items whose overlap distance is 0.5 only because of buyers below θ are not a core at ε = 0, and they are a core of that one qualifying user at ε = 0.5.
- Three users with the partial-overlap triangle (distance 0.5 on every pair) form a core of 3 at θ = 2. That group is not a biclique.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
Runtime.evaluate is being used to set files and submit.

The JSONL file is 9MB. A single CDP evaluate call will fetch the CSV and JSONL fixtures, submit the form, and poll for results until the "Products in the group" heading appears.

The script fetches the CSV and JSONL fixtures. It converts the CSV text into a File object and assigns it to the nodes input via DataTransfer. It then begins building a second DataTransfer for the JSONL blob.

The JSONL blob is added to the second DataTransfer and assigned to the form input. The form submits immediately. A 20-second polling loop checks the page body for the target ASIN and edge count, returning a snippet if found or an error if the request fails.

The polling loop now returns a timeout flag if the target ASIN and edge count do not appear within 20 seconds. The CDP evaluate call is configured with returnByValue and awaitPromise enabled. The page only adds an error class after failure, so the check will not fire prematurely.
</details></think>
